lessons.title: Why Git Matters for Data Work

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if it isn't already set up, configure your name and email with `git config --global`, then create a brand-new folder for a small SQL/dbt-style project (even a few .sql files is enough) and run `git init` inside it to confirm it becomes a real repository.
slots.deliverable: A working Git installation (confirmed with `git --version`) and a new local repository with its `.git` folder visible after `git init`.

slots.practicalActivity: In your new repository, create a file like `customer_ltv.sql`, stage it with `git add`, and make your first commit with a real message. Then run `git branch` to see your current branch, create and switch to a new branch called `rework-ltv-grain` with `git switch -c`, and make a small edit and commit it there.
slots.deliverable: A repository with at least 2 commits on main and 1 commit on a separate branch, confirmed by `git log` on each branch showing different history.

slots.practicalActivity: Switch back to main, make a conflicting edit to the same line of `customer_ltv.sql` you changed on your branch, commit it, then run `git merge rework-ltv-grain` and deliberately work through the resulting conflict markers by hand before committing the resolved merge. Separately, try `git rebase main` on a fresh branch with no conflicts to see the difference in resulting history.
slots.deliverable: A real resolved merge conflict (confirmed by the file's final content and `git log --graph`), plus a clean rebase performed on a separate conflict-free branch.

slots.practicalActivity: Branching drill: create 3 short-lived branches off main in a row, each making one small change to a different file, merging each one back before starting the next — then deliberately create one more conflict on purpose and resolve it without looking back at the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A repository history (visible via `git log --graph --all`) showing 3 clean branch-and-merge cycles plus one resolved conflict, all done independently.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a new private repository on GitHub, add it as a remote to your local repository with `git remote add origin`, then push your existing commits with `git push -u origin main`. Make one more commit locally and push it, then clone the same repo into a second folder and confirm `git pull` picks up changes made from the first copy.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub repository containing your pushed commit history, plus a second local clone confirmed in sync via `git pull`.

slots.practicalActivity: Push a new branch with at least one real commit, then open a pull request on GitHub against main (using the 'Compare & pull request' banner), writing a real description of what changed and why. Add at least one inline line comment and one suggested change on your own diff to practice the review mechanics before merging it.
slots.deliverable: A merged pull request on GitHub with a written description and at least one line comment with a suggested change, visible in the PR's history.

slots.practicalActivity: Create 3 GitHub Issues describing small, realistic tasks for your project (e.g. 'add a .gitignore', 'fix a broken model reference', 'write a GitHub Actions workflow'), then set up a Project board with To Do / In Progress / Done columns and move one issue through all three states as you actually complete it.
slots.deliverable: 3 real GitHub Issues and a Project board with at least one issue dragged through To Do, In Progress, and Done, linked to the commit or PR that closed it.

lessons.title: Notebooks in Git: The Diff Problem

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real .gitignore for a data project covering target/, dbt_packages/, logs/, .env, and any local CSV/output files you don't want committed, then test it by creating one file matching each pattern and confirming `git status` ignores them. If you have a .ipynb notebook, commit it, change only its output cells, and inspect the resulting diff to see the JSON-noise problem firsthand.
slots.deliverable: A working .gitignore confirmed to exclude every listed pattern via `git status`, plus a real notebook diff showing the output-cell noise problem.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git LFS, run `git lfs install` and `git lfs track` on one file type you'd realistically have in a data project (e.g. a sample .csv or .parquet file), commit it, and confirm with `git lfs ls-files` that it's tracked by LFS rather than stored as a normal blob. Then organize a small mixed SQL + dbt + notebook project under one repository following this chapter's versioning guidance.
slots.deliverable: A repository with at least one file tracked through Git LFS (confirmed via `git lfs ls-files`), inside a repo that also version-controls SQL, dbt models, and a notebook.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph explanation, in your own words, of the difference between Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment using your own project as the example (what would get tested on every PR vs. what would get deployed on merge to main), then sketch the pipeline as a short YAML-like outline on paper before writing any real workflow file.
slots.deliverable: A written CI vs. CD explanation grounded in your own project, plus a hand-sketched outline of the pipeline you're about to build.

lessons.title: Running Tests Automatically on Every Commit

slots.practicalActivity: Add a minimal workflow file to `.github/workflows/` in your repository, triggered on push, with at least two `echo` steps, push it, then find the resulting run on the Actions tab and read the expanded step logs to confirm each step ran in order. Then add a real third step that runs a test command relevant to your project (a Python test, a SQL lint, or a simple assertion script).
slots.deliverable: A committed GitHub Actions workflow with a passing run visible on the Actions tab, including at least one real automated test step beyond the echo commands.

slots.practicalActivity: GitHub Actions drill: without copying the lesson's YAML, write a second workflow from scratch that triggers only on pull_request (not push), checks out the repo with actions/checkout, and runs a command of your choosing — then open a real PR and confirm it appears as a status check before you're allowed to merge.
slots.deliverable: A second, original GitHub Actions workflow triggered on pull_request, visible as a required or informational status check on a real PR.

lessons.chapterTitle: Building a CI/CD Pipeline for a Data Project

slots.practicalActivity: Build a complete GitHub Actions workflow for a dbt project (your own, or the dbt course's capstone project if you've taken it): write a `profiles.yml` from environment variables inside the workflow, install dbt, and run `dbt build --profiles-dir .` as a job step triggered on every pull request against main.
slots.deliverable: A working CI workflow that runs `dbt build` against a real dbt project on every pull request, with at least one real passing run visible on the Actions tab.

lessons.title: Environment Variables & Secrets in CI/CD
lessons.chapterTitle: Building a CI/CD Pipeline for a Data Project

slots.practicalActivity: Add a second job to your workflow, gated with `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` so it only runs on a push to main (not on PRs), using a separate `--target prod` from your CI job's `--target ci`. Store your warehouse credentials as real GitHub Secrets and reference them via `${{ secrets.* }}` instead of anything hardcoded.
slots.deliverable: A two-job workflow where the CI job runs on every PR and a separate deploy job runs only on merges to main, using GitHub Secrets for every credential.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Data Project With a Real CI/CD Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full capstone end to end against a real (or realistic practice) dbt project: a clean repository with a proper .gitignore, at least one feature built on its own branch and merged via a real pull request with a line comment and suggestion, a CI workflow running `dbt build` on every PR with one deliberately broken commit opened as a PR to prove the red X actually catches something, and a gated deploy job using real GitHub Secrets.
slots.deliverable: A GitHub repository satisfying all four capstone sections: Git hygiene, a reviewed PR, a CI job that caught a real deliberate failure, and a working gated deploy job.

slots.practicalActivity: Walk a stranger (a peer, mentor, or yourself on a recording) through the finished repository: the .gitignore and why each entry is there, the commit history and what each PR changed, the CI workflow and the specific run where it caught a real break, and the deploy job's gating logic — without any verbal explanation the repository itself couldn't already show.
slots.deliverable: A completed walkthrough (live or recorded) of the finished repository covering Git hygiene, review, CI, and deployment, plus the repository link ready for a portfolio.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can manage a real SQL/dbt/notebook project in Git and GitHub end to end — branching without breaking things, reviewing pull requests, and building a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline that tests every change on a PR and deploys automatically, with secrets handled safely, on merge to main.
